subject: zoology_2
question_text: How is respiratory movements regulated in man?

insider_note: Name all four controls in the first two lines. A student who explains only the medulla caps the answer at one mark.

page_header: Breathing and Exchange of Gases · 4 marks

steps.label: Respiratory rhythm centre
steps.why: Breathing continues in sleep, so the rhythm has to be set by a centre in the brain and not by a decision.
common_mistakes: Placing the rhythm centre in the cerebrum. It lies in the medulla oblongata.
Writing that breathing is voluntary. Only forced breathing is.
steps.memory_tip: The medulla keeps the beat of breathing.
steps.margin_note: Name all four controls first, then explain each.
lines: Except forced inhalation and exhalation,
respiratory movements are involuntary.
Respiration is regulated by four controls.
The respiratory rhythm centre lies in the
medulla oblongata of the brain.
It is mainly responsible for respiratory
movements.

steps.label: Pneumotaxic centre
steps.why: The rhythm centre alone would breathe at one fixed rate, so a second centre is needed to change the rate when the body demands it.
common_mistakes: Placing the pneumotaxic centre in the medulla. It lies in the pons.
Writing that it starts breathing. It only alters the rate.
steps.memory_tip: Pons is the pace setter; medulla is the rhythm keeper.
steps.margin_note: Two lines are enough for this control.
lines: The pneumotaxic centre lies in the pons of
the brain stem.
It sends signals to the respiratory rhythm
centre and alters the respiratory rate when
necessary.

steps.label: Chemosensitive area
steps.why: The body watches carbon dioxide rather than oxygen, because carbon dioxide changes the acidity of the blood much faster.
common_mistakes: Writing that the area is sensitive to oxygen. It responds to CO₂ and H⁺.
Leaving out what follows. The rate must increase to remove the CO₂.
steps.memory_tip: Carbon dioxide, not oxygen, is what the brain measures.
steps.margin_note: Say what it senses and what it makes the body do.
lines: A chemosensitive area lies close to the
respiratory rhythm centre.
It is sensitive to CO₂ and H⁺ ions.
When these rise in the blood it signals the
rhythm centre, which increases the
respiratory rate to remove them.

steps.label: Aortic and carotid receptors
steps.why: These receptors sit in the arteries leaving the heart, so they sample the blood before it reaches the rest of the body.
common_mistakes: Placing the receptors in the lungs. They lie in the aortic arch and carotid arteries.
Leaving out the role of oxygen here. These receptors also watch it.
steps.memory_tip: Aortic arch and carotid: the two check posts on the way out.
steps.margin_note: One boxed line makes the summary clear.
lines: Receptors lie in the aortic arch and in the
carotid arteries.
They send signals to the respiratory rhythm
centre when the CO₂ and H⁺ concentration
in the blood increases.

lines.text: Rising CO₂ is the main signal to breathe more
